zones.name: Lakes, rivers and inland seas
zones.who_owns: The countries around the water. A border lake or river is split by a treaty, and where a treaty only names a river, the line usually follows the thalweg, meaning the deepest channel. A few waters have no agreed line at all, and they still belong to the countries on the shore, never to a newcomer.

rules.cite: Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea (2018)
rules.says: Each of the five shore countries gets 24 km of territorial water and 16 km more of exclusive fishing. The rest of the surface counts as international water, and the seabed is left to deals between pairs of countries.
Pheasant Island in the Bidasoa river stays a condominium, meaning France and Spain share it. Each governs it for six months in turn.
Where an 1890 treaty named the "main channel" of the Chobe, the court worked out which channel that was. The island fell on the Botswana side.

rules.cite: Kenya Colony and Protectorate Order in Council (1926)
rules.says: A colonial order draws the Kenya-Uganda line across Lake Victoria by straight lines between named islands. It is copied into the Ugandan constitution and was used to place Migingo in 2009.
No binding agreement fixes the borders in the deep part of the lake. Areas under 25 m deep go to the nearest country, and shipping and fishing have treaties of their own.

zones.hook: Lake police and customs from the nearest shore. On Migingo, Uganda sold special permits to residents and posted 48 police officers. Caspian patrol boats have fired on survey vessels.
zones.can_you_build: Only with the permission of the country that holds the spot. A treaty you are not party to can reassign a river island, as Lausanne did to Ada Kaleh in 1923, and a dam can drown it, as happened there in 1970. On Pheasant Island, access itself is forbidden.
facts: Caspian Sea area: 389,000 km2, five shore countries
Caspian convention signed 12 August 2018 at Aktau: 24 km of territorial water plus 16 km of exclusive fishing
Pheasant Island in January 2018: about 200 m by 40 m, uninhabited, eroding
Migingo: about 2,000 m2 with 131 people reported in 2009; Ugandan police estimated about 500
Migingo lies 510 m on the Kenyan side of the line, per the July 2009 survey
Sedudu: about 5 km2, flooded for several months each year

zones.name: New land: volcanic islands, sandbars and rising ground
zones.who_owns: Almost always the country whose waters the ground rises in, because that country already holds the seabed there. Land that rises from a seabed no one holds has only one tested case, Graham Island in 1831, and it sank before anyone won. Land built by people has weaker status than land made by nature.

rules.says: An island is land that formed naturally, has water all round it, and stays above water at high tide.
Rocks that cannot support people living there or an economy of their own get no exclusive economic zone or continental shelf.
A coastal country holds sovereignty over its territorial sea and the seabed below it, so a volcano that surfaces there rises on ground it already holds.
Artificial islands are not islands in law. They get no territorial sea and do not move any maritime line.

rules.cite: Bay of Bengal Maritime Boundary Arbitration (Bangladesh v India), 2014
rules.says: The tribunal drew the sea boundary and left the site of vanished South Talpatti on the Indian side.

zones.hook: A navy reaches new ground within days. In 1831 a Sicilian customs official landed by 17 July and a British captain by 2 August. In 1963 Iceland answered a joke French claim on Surtsey at once, and the state then closed the island to almost everyone.
zones.can_you_build: In practice no. New ash and silt wash away: Graham lasted about six months, Zalzala Koh about three years, and the merged Hunga island seven. Surtsey, which did harden, is a nature reserve where only a few scientists may land.
facts: Graham Island 1831: about 4 km2 and 63 m high at its peak, gone by January 1832
Surtsey: began 14 November 1963, ended 5 June 1967, highest point then 174 m
Hunga Tonga and Hunga Haʻapai joined in 2015 and were destroyed in January 2022
South Talpatti: appeared after the November 1970 cyclone, never above 2 m, gone around March 2010
Zalzala Koh: rose 24 September 2013, about 2 km offshore, gone by end of 2016
Fonuafoʻou: appeared 14 October 1885, collapsed 1949, now 17 m under water

sources.t: UNCLOS Part VIII, Regime of islands, United Nations

zones.name: Icebergs, ice shelves and drifting ice
zones.who_owns: No settled answer. Writers on the law take three views of a free-floating iceberg: it belongs to no one (res nullius, the Latin term), it can be held under a claim by a state, or it is shared by all (res communis). Ice shelves around Antarctica fall inside the Antarctic Treaty area.

rules.says: The treaty covers everything south of 60 degrees South, including all ice shelves, without taking away rights any country has on the high seas in that area.
Argues that an iceberg floating free in Antarctic waters is no state's property and sits on the high seas, so taking and towing it would rather not breach any state's territorial rights.

rules.cite: Flag of the ship (see ships-flag zone)
rules.says: A towing ship answers to its flag country. The same article notes the UAE is party to neither the Antarctic Treaty System nor UNCLOS, which leaves open how far those rules bind a UAE-flagged tow.

zones.hook: The supply line. Nobody needs to board the ice: Norway reached Camp Barneo by restricting flights from Svalbard. For how a court treated a killing on drifting ice, see Fletcher's Ice Island T-3, already on this map.
zones.can_you_build: Yes for weeks or years, never for good. Camp Barneo was rebuilt from scratch every April because the ice moves. Soviet and Russian stations usually ran two or three years on one floe, and since the mid-2000s several were evacuated early because the ice thawed too fast. Max Perutz warned in 1942 that natural icebergs have too little surface above water for an airstrip and can roll over.
facts: A23a: about 3,500 km2 in January 2025, 180 km2 by March 2026
North Pole-1: 9 months and 2,850 km of drift in 1937-38
Some 800 people have drifted on North Pole stations since 1937
Barneo: from about $20,000 a visit, drift of 0.8 km/h recorded in 2007
Project Habakkuk: planned length 600 m; pykrete needed cooling to -16 C
UAE Iceberg Project estimate: $100-150 million

sources.t: Osiecki, United Arab Emirates "Iceberg Project": would an ambitious concept comply with international law?, Ius Novum 2/2022

zones.name: Underground and under the seabed
zones.who_owns: Whoever holds the surface above. A country's sovereignty runs down from its land and its territorial sea. Past that, a coastal country keeps rights in the subsoil of its continental shelf, and it can tunnel there at any depth of water. A private landowner may own the ground below, though in many places minerals beyond a set depth belong to the state.

rules.says: A coastal country's sovereignty reaches the bed and subsoil of its territorial sea.
The continental shelf is the seabed and subsoil beyond the territorial sea, out to the edge of the continental margin or to 200 nautical miles.
The coastal country alone may explore the shelf and take its resources, and nobody else may do so without its express consent, even if it never uses them.
The shelf rules do not limit a coastal country's right to exploit the subsoil by tunnelling, however deep the water above.
Whoever owns the soil owns up to the sky and down to the depths. Modern law keeps a limited form and often separates mineral rights from the land title.

zones.hook: Ordinary police, fire and licensing law. A bunker has an address, so the state simply walks in. The local Dutch town refused CyberBunker a business licence after a 2002 fire, German investigators tapped its traffic under a warrant from 2015, and 600 police raided its second bunker in 2019.
zones.can_you_build: Yes, as private property under local law. Buying the land is the easy part: Survival Condo paid $300,000 for a silo. Geology and safety rules still bind you. Vivos dropped its largest project in 2014 over the stability of a former mine. No thickness of rock changes which country you are in.
facts: CyberBunker bunker at Kloetinge: 20,000 sq ft, built 1955, bought 1995
Pionen: 30 m of granite over 1,100 m2 in central Stockholm
Survival Condo: silo 197 ft deep, 15 floors, 12 units, about $20 million by 2012
Vivos: 575 bunkers at the former Black Hills Ordnance Depot, South Dakota
Vivos at Atchison, Kansas: planned for 5,000 people in a 2,700,000 sq ft former mine, cancelled June 2014

sources.t: UNCLOS Part VI, Continental shelf, United Nations
Cuius est solum, eius est usque ad coelum et ad inferos, Wikipedia

cases.name: Convention on the Legal Status of the Caspian Sea
cases.anchor: Centre of the Caspian Sea, as given on the source page. The convention was signed at Aktau, Kazakhstan.
cases.founder: Russia, Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Turkmenistan and Iran
cases.recognition: Signed by all five shore countries
cases.story: The Caspian covers 389,000 square kilometres, and for decades its neighbours argued over whether it counted as a sea or a lake. Under an old treaty between Iran and the Soviet Union it was treated as a lake split into two sectors, with fish shared. When the Soviet Union ended, four new or renewed shore states replaced it on that side. Russia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan made deals with each other using median lines, meaning lines halfway between shores. Iran wanted a single deal among all five and aimed for a one-fifth share. Iranian patrol boats at times fired on vessels Azerbaijan sent to explore disputed fields. Talks ran from about 1990 to 2018. On 12 August 2018 at Aktau, the five leaders signed a convention giving each country 24 kilometres of territorial water and 16 kilometres more of exclusive fishing. The rest of the surface is international water. The seabed, which holds the oil and gas, stays undefined and is left to deals between countries.
cases.mechanism: The convention treats the Caspian as neither fully a sea nor a lake, so its open middle is shared by five named countries and offers an outsider none of the freedoms of the ocean.

cases.name: Lake Constance, the lake with no agreed border
cases.founder: Germany, Switzerland and Austria
cases.recognition: Three countries hold three different views
cases.story: Lake Constance lies where Germany, Switzerland and Austria meet. Its shores run through the German states of Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria, the Swiss cantons of St. Gallen, Thurgau and Schaffhausen, and the Austrian state of Vorarlberg. Areas less than 25 metres deep are treated as belonging to the nearest country. Beyond that depth, no legally binding agreement says where the borders run. Switzerland holds that the line goes down the middle of the lake. Austria says the disputed part belongs to all the shore states together, an arrangement known as a condominium. Germany has kept its opinion ambiguous. Because the three cannot settle the map, shipping and fishing are handled by separate treaties, so daily life on the water goes on without a line. The result is a large stretch of water with no drawn border in the middle of Europe. Under each of the three national views, the deep water still belongs to one or more of the shore countries, so the missing line opens nothing to an outsider.
cases.mechanism: A missing border between neighbours leaves a dispute among them, and the water still belongs to one or more of the shore states under every view they hold.

cases.name: Pheasant Island
cases.founder: France and Spain, by the Treaty of the Pyrenees
cases.story: Pheasant Island sits in the Bidasoa river between Irun in Spain and Hendaye in France. In 1659 it hosted 24 conferences between Spain's Luis Méndez de Haro and France's Cardinal Mazarin that ended in the Treaty of the Pyrenees. Under that treaty the island stays a condominium, meaning the two countries share sovereignty. They take turns. The naval commander at Hondarribia governs it from 1 February to 31 July, and a French official carrying the title "viceroy of Pheasant Island" governs it from 1 August to 31 January. In practice the mayors of Irun and Hendaye handle it. In January 2018 it measured about 200 metres by 40 metres, and it was eroding. Nobody lives there and access is forbidden, apart from rare heritage open days. Municipal staff land every six months to clean and garden, and naval personnel from San Sebastián and Bayonne check it every five days. It is an example of a border river island that has been held under a shared treaty for more than three centuries.
cases.mechanism: A treaty can give a river island to two countries at once, which means two sets of officials hold the right to remove anyone who lands.

cases.name: Migingo Island
cases.founder: Ugandan marine police (flag raised); earlier Kenyan and Ugandan fishermen settled
cases.stopped_by: Joint Kenya-Uganda border survey, July 2009
cases.pop: 131 reported in 2009; Ugandan police estimated about 500
cases.recognition: Kenyan, per the 2009 survey and President Museveni
cases.story: Migingo is a rock of about 2,000 square metres in Lake Victoria, valued for the Nile perch around it. Two Kenyan fishermen say they settled it in 1991. A Ugandan fisherman says he arrived in 2004. Kenya said that in June 2004 Ugandan marine police pitched a tent and raised a flag. In February 2009 Kenyans living there were told to buy special Ugandan permits, which set off a diplomatic row. On 13 March 2009 ministers met in Kampala and agreed that Uganda would withdraw its 48 police officers. A visit two weeks later ended in insults over the police staying. Uganda proposed a survey using a 1926 colonial order, copied into its constitution, which draws the line between named islands. In May, President Museveni conceded the island was Kenyan. A joint survey began on 2 June, and its results in late July placed Migingo 510 metres inside Kenya. Uganda then lowered its flag and withdrew. In 2009 the rock held homes of corrugated metal, four pubs, a pharmacy and an open-air casino.
cases.mechanism: An old colonial line copied into a constitution decided the island, and a joint survey on the water put it into effect; first settlement and a raised flag did not change the result.

cases.name: Ada Kaleh
cases.founder: Overlooked at the 1878 Congress of Berlin
cases.stopped_by: Treaty of Lausanne, 1923, then flooded by the Iron Gates dam in 1970
cases.story: Ada Kaleh was a Danube island about 1.75 kilometres long, just downstream of Orșova. Austria and the Ottoman Empire fought over its fortress for a century. When peace was negotiated at the Congress of Berlin in 1878, the delegates forgot it. Ottoman land on both banks was lost, but the island stayed an Ottoman possession in law, with Austria-Hungary controlling one side of the river and Serbia the other. The Ottoman government kept sending an administrator and a judge. Residents paid no tax or customs, were not subject to conscription, and voted in the Ottoman general elections of 1908. The island became known as a free port and a smugglers' nest, and it made Turkish delight and rose oil. Austria-Hungary declared sovereignty over it in 1913, Romania occupied it in 1919, and the Treaty of Lausanne made it Romanian in 1923. The remaining Turkish residents emigrated by 1967. Construction of the Iron Gates hydroelectric plant submerged the island in 1970.
cases.mechanism: A river island left out of a peace treaty stayed with its old sovereign for 45 years as a tax-free exclave, until the Treaty of Lausanne gave it to Romania.

cases.name: Kasikili/Sedudu Island case
cases.founder: Botswana and Namibia, by Special Agreement
cases.stopped_by: International Court of Justice ruling, 1999
cases.story: Sedudu, called Kasikili in Namibia, is an island of about 5 square kilometres in the Chobe River. No one lives there permanently, and floods cover it for several months a year from about March. It sits on the border because of an 1890 treaty between Germany and Britain, the Heligoland-Zanzibar Treaty, which settled their colonies in what are now Namibia and Botswana. The treaty put the line in the "main channel" of the river without saying which channel that was. In 1996 the two countries signed a Special Agreement asking the International Court of Justice to decide the boundary and the island's status. The court studied the river and held in 1999 that the northern channel must be regarded as the main one. The line therefore follows the thalweg, the deepest part of the channel, north of the island, which places Sedudu in Botswana. The island is now one of the top tourist attractions in the Chobe area.
cases.mechanism: The International Court of Justice settled who holds a river island by deciding which channel a colonial treaty meant, and then following its deepest line.

cases.name: Santa Rosa Island, Amazon River
cases.founder: Congress of Peru
cases.challenge: Colombia protests and seeks bilateral allocation of islands
cases.recognition: Administered by Peru; disputed by Colombia
cases.story: Santa Rosa is a river island in the Amazon at the point where Brazil, Colombia and Peru meet, across the water from Leticia in Colombia and Tabatinga in Brazil. About 3,000 people live there, under Peruvian administration going back decades. In June 2025 Peru's Congress made the island a district of its Loreto region. On 5 August 2025 Colombian President Gustavo Petro said that Peru had "appropriated it by law". Peru relies on treaties from 1922 and 1929, and treats the island as an extension of Chinería Island. Colombia answers that Santa Rosa had not yet emerged from the river when those treaties were signed, so they cannot have assigned it. It also argues that the border follows the deepest line of the Amazon and that new islands have formed on its side. Colombia's foreign ministry says the two countries need to work together on allocating islands. Petro warned the change could cut Leticia, with nearly 60,000 people, off from the river. The island remains listed as disputed, and the riverbanks there keep shifting.
cases.mechanism: When a river makes new land after a border treaty, nothing in the treaty may say who gets it, and two neighbouring states then compete for it through statutes and diplomatic notes.

sources.t: Al Jazeera, Colombia's President Petro accuses Peru of annexing disputed Amazon island, 5 Aug 2025

cases.name: Graham Island
cases.founder: Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, Britain, France and Spain, as rival claimants
cases.stopped_by: The sea: the island eroded away
cases.story: In July 1831 a submarine volcano about 30 kilometres south of Sicily broke the surface. By 17 July a Sicilian customs official, Michele Fiorini, had landed and planted an oar to claim the islet for the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies. On 2 August Captain Humphrey Senhouse of the Royal Navy claimed it for Britain and named it after Sir James Graham, First Lord of the Admiralty. Britain thought it could help control Mediterranean shipping. King Ferdinand sent the corvette Etna and called it Ferdinandea. The French geologist Constant Prévost named it Julia, and Spain also declared an interest. At its largest it was about 4 square kilometres and 63 metres high, with two small lakes. Tourists came to see it. It was made of loose ash, which waves wore down, and officials reported no trace by 17 December. Its summit now sits a few metres under water. When it stirred again in 2002, Italian sailors put a flag on the top of the bank to head off future claims.
cases.mechanism: Four rival claims to land rising outside any agreed water never reached a ruling because the island sank within about six months, so the question of who owns such land stayed open.

cases.name: Surtsey and the Paris Match landing
cases.founder: Natural eruption; Iceland asserted title
cases.stopped_by: Iceland, which declared it a nature reserve in 1965
cases.challenge: A joking French claim, answered at once by Iceland
cases.story: On 14 November 1963 the cook of the trawler Ísleifur II saw dark smoke off southern Iceland and the crew found an eruption breaching the sea. An Icelandic naming committee called the new island Surtsey after a fire giant in Norse myth. On 6 December three French journalists from Paris Match landed and stayed about 15 minutes, until explosions drove them off. They jokingly claimed the island for France. Iceland quickly asserted that it belonged to Iceland. The eruption ran until 5 June 1967, with hard lava capping the loose ash, so the island survived where many others wash away. Its highest point then was 174 metres. Iceland declared it a nature reserve in 1965, while it was still erupting, so scientists could watch life arrive on bare rock. Only a few scientists may land today, and everyone else can view it closely only from a small plane. Iceland has kept that rule in place, so no one has been able to settle the island.
cases.mechanism: New land off a coastal state's shore is treated as that state's from the start, and the state can close it by a conservation order before anyone settles.

cases.name: Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai island
cases.founder: Natural eruption, 2014-15
cases.stopped_by: The eruption of January 2022
cases.story: Hunga Tonga and Hunga Haʻapai were two small islands on the rim of a submarine volcano, about 1.6 kilometres apart and 65 kilometres north of Tonga's main island, Tongatapu. An eruption in 2014 and 2015 built new ground that joined them into one island, with a strip of deposits 380 metres wide, called a tombolo, linking one side. Surveys in 2019 found ferns, guava trees, mosses and sedges, along with cockroaches, moths, rats and spiders. Grass, coconuts and bush covered the older parts, and seabirds bred there. The highest point, in the former Hunga Tonga, reached 149 metres. In January 2022 the volcano erupted again, sending a plume 58 kilometres high and a tsunami as far as Japan and the Americas. The eruption destroyed the joined island. For about seven years it had met the plain test in the law of the sea for an island: formed naturally, with water all round, and above high tide. Plants, insects and birds had arrived in that time.
cases.mechanism: Under UNCLOS Article 121, land formed naturally and above high tide counts as an island, a status that lasts only as long as the land does.

sources.t: UNCLOS Part VIII, Regime of islands, United Nations

cases.name: Nishinoshima
cases.founder: Natural eruptions, 1973 and 2013
cases.story: Nishinoshima was a small green island about 940 kilometres south-southeast of Tokyo and 130 kilometres from the nearest inhabited Ogasawara island. On 30 May 1973 a fishing boat told the Japan Coast Guard it had seen white smoke rising nearby. The Coast Guard flew over the same day, and it went on surveying from the air as new land formed. By August 1974 it put the new island's area at about 316,000 square metres. Erosion and shifting sand then joined the new ground to the old. A further eruption began in November 2013 and built another islet to the southeast. Officials said it would be named once it was stable and clearly going to stay, but it merged with the main island first. By July 2016 a cone stood about 142 metres high. Further eruptions followed in 2020, 2021 and 2022. A Japanese agency has watched this process at every stage, so the new ground has simply been added to an island the state already held.
cases.mechanism: When new land grows onto an island a state already holds, it adds to that state's territory, and no separate question of ownership arises.

cases.name: Zalzala Koh
cases.founder: Natural event, 7.7-magnitude earthquake
cases.stopped_by: The sea
cases.story: On 24 September 2013 a 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck Balochistan in Pakistan, and within hours a small island appeared in the Arabian Sea. Its name means "Earthquake Mountain" in Urdu. It stood about 2 kilometres from shore, near Gwadar and the Hingol area, close enough to be seen from the coast. It may have been a mud volcano. The head of Pakistan's National Institute of Oceanography said gas escaping from the seabed had caused it. Satellite measurements put it at about 175 metres by 160 metres and 15 to 20 metres high, though those figures were debated. Geologists predicted it would not last. It had sunk 3 metres within a month, and by the end of 2016 it was gone. While it stood, the surface was lifeless but fish and coral gathered around it, which helped local fishing. At 2 kilometres from the coast, it rose well inside waters that Pakistan already held, so no outside claim could have had any footing.
cases.mechanism: Land rising 2 kilometres offshore comes up inside the coastal state's territorial sea, whose seabed UNCLOS Article 2 already gives to that state.

cases.name: South Talpatti / New Moore Island
cases.founder: Natural sandbar; India and Bangladesh as claimants
cases.stopped_by: Sea level rise and erosion; arbitration award of 2014
cases.challenge: Bangladesh filed in October 2009; final award July 2014
cases.recognition: Award placed it on the Indian side
cases.story: This sandbar in the Bay of Bengal formed from silt after the Bhola cyclone of November 1970. A US satellite picked it up in 1974 at about 2,500 square metres. It later grew to about 10,000 square metres at low tide and never stood more than 2 metres above the sea. It lay 2 kilometres from the mouth of the Hariabhanga River, the border between India and Bangladesh. Their boundary follows the river's main channel, so the case turned on which side of the sandbar the channel ran, with each country holding its own surveys. India reportedly raised its flag in 1981 and set up a temporary Border Security Force base. Neither built anything lasting, because delta floods reshaped the ground every year. Bangladesh took the dispute to arbitration in October 2009. In March 2010 an Indian oceanographer reported the island had disappeared. The final award of 7 July 2014 gave Bangladesh 19,467 of 25,000 square kilometres of disputed sea, and left the vanished sandbar on India's side.
cases.mechanism: A sandbar too low and unstable to settle still mattered because it might have moved a sea boundary, and an arbitration tribunal ruled on its site after it had gone under.

cases.name: Fonuafoʻou
cases.founder: Natural eruption
cases.stopped_by: The 1949 eruption and collapse
cases.story: Fonuafoʻou means "new land" in Tongan. It is a submarine volcano in the western Haʻapai group of Tonga that has made an island several times. The crew of the British ship HMS Falcon first spotted the site in 1867, when it was still a coral reef. On 11 October 1885 the volcano erupted, and three days later an island stood there, which the British named Falcon Island. Eruptions in 1894, 1921, 1927, 1928, 1933 and 1936 kept building it. By 1949 it was reported at 6 kilometres across and 145 metres high. That year another eruption blew the island apart and it collapsed under the sea. Further eruptions came in 1970 and 1993, and the top now lies 17 metres below the surface. Over about 64 years the ground had looked permanent enough to get a British name and a Tongan one. Anyone relying on this ground in 1948 would have lost it the following year.
cases.mechanism: Volcanic land can appear and vanish repeatedly at one spot, and under UNCLOS Article 121 it counts as an island only during the periods when it stays above high tide.

sources.t: UNCLOS Part VIII, Regime of islands, United Nations

cases.name: Iceberg A23a
cases.anchor: Marker is near South Georgia, where the iceberg grounded in March 2025. It calved from the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf and has since broken up.
cases.founder: Natural calving
cases.stopped_by: Melt and break-up in warmer water
cases.story: A23a broke from the Filchner-Ronne Ice Shelf in Antarctica in 1986. The Soviet research base Druzhnaya I was on that part of the shelf, so the base was carried off on the iceberg, and a rescue mission began in 1987 to move it. Rusted debris from the base was still visible in the edge of the ice in January 2025. The iceberg stuck on the sea bed for many years and began moving in 2020. In January 2025 it measured about 3,500 square kilometres, the largest in the world. It spun over a seamount through much of 2024, then grounded 73 kilometres from South Georgia in March 2025 and moved off again by July. By September 2025 it was breaking up, and in March 2026 it was down to 180 square kilometres. Monitoring then stopped, and by July 2026 it was thought to be gone or nearly so. So a national base moved from an ice shelf to open ocean with no one choosing it.
cases.mechanism: A piece of ice shelf that breaks away carries everything on it out of the fixed Antarctic map, and an iceberg this large still lasted only about 40 years.

sources.t: Osiecki, United Arab Emirates "Iceberg Project": would an ambitious concept comply with international law?, Ius Novum 2/2022

cases.name: UAE Iceberg Project
cases.anchor: Marker is the Fujairah coast, the planned destination. The iceberg was to come from near Heard Island.
cases.founder: Abdulla Alsheni, National Adviser Bureau Limited
cases.recognition: None needed or sought; legal position untested
cases.story: In 2017 Abdulla Alsheni, an Emirati businessman who owned National Adviser Bureau Limited, announced a plan to tow a large iceberg from the area of Heard Island to the coast of Fujairah. In 1977 Saudi Arabia's Prince Mohammad al Faisal had set up a company, Iceberg Transport International, with the same idea, and that plan was never carried out. Alsheni presented his project to two UAE ministries, with a trial planned for early 2022 and a final tow in late 2023. The cost estimate was $100 to 150 million. The iceberg might yield 20 billion gallons of fresh water. The project's website claimed that under the freedom of the high seas, icebergs can be taken for private use anywhere. In a 2022 article in Ius Novum, Mateusz Osiecki tested that claim. He concluded a free-floating iceberg is probably no state's property, noted that writers have taken three different views, and set out the duties under the 1991 Environmental Protocol to the Antarctic Treaty. He also noted that the UAE belongs to neither the treaty system nor UNCLOS.
cases.mechanism: No treaty names the owner of a floating iceberg, so a private tow would rest on an argument from the freedom of the high seas that no court has tested.

sources.t: Osiecki, United Arab Emirates "Iceberg Project": would an ambitious concept comply with international law?, Ius Novum 2/2022

cases.name: Project Habakkuk
cases.anchor: Marker is Patricia Lake near Jasper, Alberta, where the small prototype was built. The ship was meant for the mid-Atlantic.
cases.founder: Geoffrey Pyke, for British Combined Operations
cases.stopped_by: Habakkuk board, December 1943, on cost and technical grounds
cases.story: During the Second World War, Geoffrey Pyke of Britain's Combined Operations proposed levelling an iceberg, natural or artificial, into a mid-Atlantic aircraft base beyond the reach of land-based planes. Max Perutz warned in 1942 that real icebergs have too little surface above water and can roll over. The idea survived because of pykrete, a frozen mix of water and wood pulp that was stronger and slower to melt than ice. The plan became a ship 600 metres long. Pykrete still sagged slowly unless it was kept at minus 16 degrees Celsius, so the vessel would need insulation and refrigeration. A prototype 18 metres by 9 metres, weighing 1,000 tons, was built on Patricia Lake in Alberta. The estimate grew from £700,000 to £2.5 million, and Canada said it could not be done that season. The Habakkuk board last met in December 1943 and called the large ship impractical. As planned, it would have been a British aircraft carrier.
cases.mechanism: The largest ice platform ever seriously planned needed constant refrigeration and a government budget, and it would have been a warship under one state's flag with no separate status of its own.

cases.name: North Pole drifting ice stations
cases.anchor: Marker is the start of North Pole-1, about 20 km from the Pole. Each station drifted for months or years.
cases.founder: Soviet Union and Russia, through the Arctic and Antarctic Research Institute
cases.pop: Some 800 people across all stations since 1937, replaced yearly
cases.story: On 21 May 1937 the Soviet Union set up North Pole-1 on an ice floe about 20 kilometres from the Pole. Otto Schmidt led the expedition. Four men lived there for 9 months while the floe drifted 2,850 kilometres, and icebreakers took them off on 19 February 1938. They came home as Heroes of the Soviet Union. From 1954, one to three stations ran each year, and a typical camp began in April and lasted two or three years until the floe reached the Greenland Sea. North Pole-22 drifted for nine years. The program stopped after the Soviet Union ended and resumed in 2003. From the mid-2000s it became hard to find a safe floe, and several stations were evacuated early because the ice thawed too quickly. Russia then ordered a self-propelled, ice-resistant platform called North Pole from Admiralty Shipyard in 2017, to replace camps on bare ice. It was completed in August 2022, ran station NP-41 from 2022 to 2024, and started NP-42 in 2024. All of these stations have been run by one government institute.
cases.mechanism: People can live on drifting sea ice for years under a state institute's supply chain, and thinning ice has now led that state to put its station on a vessel.

cases.name: Camp Barneo
cases.anchor: 2007 camp position, about 48 km from the Pole. The camp was rebuilt on new ice each year.
cases.founder: Alexander Orlov; later Irina Orlova, then Frederik Paulsen
cases.stopped_by: Norwegian flight limits, the Russia-Ukraine dispute, COVID-19 and the 2022 invasion of Ukraine
cases.pop: Tourists and staff, a few weeks each April
cases.recognition: None; run under patronage of the Russian Geographical Society
cases.story: Camp Barneo was a private tourist camp on Arctic Ocean ice near the North Pole. The Russian Alexander Orlov founded it in 2002. His widow Irina Orlova ran it after him until selling it to the Swedish billionaire Frederik Paulsen. Each April it was rebuilt from nothing, because the ice keeps moving. In 2007 winds pushed the camp southeast at 0.8 kilometres an hour. A visit cost about $20,000. From 2002 to 2017, every trip started and ended at Longyearbyen on Svalbard, which is part of Norway. That gave Norway a handle on a camp sitting on ice beyond any country. In 2016, after Chechen paratroopers held military exercises at Barneo, Norway imposed a flight embargo that it later lifted. A dispute between Russia and Ukraine stopped tourist flights in 2019, and COVID-19 cancelled 2020 and 2021. Plans for 2022 ended with the Russian invasion of Ukraine. A 2024 season to leave from Russia was also cancelled, and the camp has stood vacant since 2018.
cases.mechanism: A camp on drifting ice beyond any country still depends on an airport, so the country holding that airport can shut it down without going near the ice.

cases.name: CyberBunker
cases.founder: Herman-Johan Xennt
cases.stopped_by: German police raid, September 2019; convictions in 2021
cases.laws: Own rule: any site except child abuse material and terrorism
cases.challenge: Yes. Lost in Hamburg in 2010; convicted in Germany in 2021
cases.story: In 1995 Herman-Johan Xennt bought a 20,000-square-foot former NATO bunker near Kloetinge in the Netherlands, built in 1955 to survive a nuclear attack. He ran a web-hosting firm there that took any site except child abuse material and terrorism. Its spokesman, Sven Olaf Kamphuis, called it the Republic of CyberBunker and styled himself Minister of Telecommunications and Foreign Affairs. In 2002 a fire exposed an MDMA lab, three men were jailed, and the town refused a business licence. The firm moved its servers above ground and kept advertising the bunker. A Hamburg court barred it from hosting The Pirate Bay in 2010, and Dutch prosecutors had Kamphuis arrested in Spain in 2013 over an attack on Spamhaus. That year it bought a second bunker at Traben-Trarbach in Germany. Investigators tapped its traffic from 2015, and an undercover gardener and cleaner went in. In September 2019, 600 police raided it. In 2021 Xennt and six others were convicted of forming a criminal organisation and got 28 to 59 months.
cases.mechanism: Calling a bunker a republic gives it no legal status, and the state above it applied its licensing, wiretap and criminal law to everything inside.

cases.name: Pionen data centre
cases.founder: Bahnhof, Swedish internet provider
cases.story: Pionen is a civil defence centre built in 1943 in the White Mountains in the Södermalm district of Stockholm, to protect government functions in wartime. The Swedish internet provider Bahnhof converted it into a data centre, which opened on 11 September 2008. It lies under 30 metres of granite, behind a door 40 centimetres thick, and can be reached only by an entrance tunnel, and it is described as able to withstand a hydrogen bomb. It covers 1,100 square metres and has greenhouses, fountains, simulated daylight and a large saltwater fish tank. Its two backup generators are submarine engines. Bahnhof also rents rack space there to others, and in 2010 WikiLeaks kept servers in the site. HavenCo, on Sealand and already on this map, sold a similar hardened home for data from a fort at sea, and it relied on a claim of independence. Pionen stands at Renstiernas gata 35 and 37 in central Stockholm, inside Sweden, under ordinary Swedish government and law.
cases.mechanism: A hardened site protects servers physically, and all of its legal protection comes from the law of the country above it.

cases.name: Vivos shelters
cases.anchor: Marker is the former Black Hills Ordnance Depot, South Dakota, the largest site.
cases.founder: Robert Vicino
cases.pop: Company claims about 100,000 members and over 1,000 buyers, September 2022
cases.recognition: Private real estate under US law
cases.story: Vivos is a California company founded by Robert Vicino that sells places in underground shelters for use after a disaster. Its first completed shelter, in Indiana, dates from the Cold War and was built to withstand a near direct hit from a 20-megaton bomb. It holds 80 people. In 2016 the company took over shelters built in 1967 at the former Black Hills Ordnance Depot in South Dakota, where it lists 575 bunkers of about 2,150 square feet each. It also planned to convert a Soviet-built complex at Rothenstein in Germany for 1,000 people, where fire rules were expected to require sprinklers throughout. In 2013 Vivos acquired purchase rights to part of a former limestone mine at Atchison, Kansas, owned earlier by the US Army, for 5,000 people. It cancelled that in June 2014 after Army geologists raised concerns about collapses. As of September 2022, Vicino said the firm had about 100,000 members and over 1,000 buyers. These figures come from the company.
cases.mechanism: Vivos sells underground space as ordinary property, so German fire codes and US geological reviews apply to it as they would to any building above ground.

cases.name: Survival Condo
cases.founder: Larry Hall
cases.pop: Capacity up to 75; no owners in residence in 2020
cases.challenge: Lawsuit over a $3 million loan, settled in August 2019
cases.recognition: Kansas real estate, owned by a not-for-profit company
cases.cost: Silo bought for $300,000; about $20 million development
cases.story: In 2008 Larry Hall bought a disused Atlas missile silo at Raven Ridge near Concordia, Kansas, for $300,000. The silo goes down 197 feet. He built a 15-floor bunker with 12 condominium units for up to 75 people, plus a swimming pool, theatre, library, gym, climbing wall, vegetable gardens, fish tanks and three years of stored food. It also has armouries, a sniper post with a remote-controlled rifle and a jail cell. Development finished by 2012 at a cost of $20 million. Hall said all units had sold by 2017, though 6 appeared for sale in 2020, and no owners were living there that year. Ordinary law reached it in the usual way. Peter Ziegler, who bought Unit 5 in 2013, lent the company $3 million. After he died in 2017, his estate sued in January 2019, saying assets had been moved to other companies, and the parties settled that August. The facility is owned by a Kansas not-for-profit company, incorporated in 2012.
cases.mechanism: Buying a missile silo gives you ordinary title to land in Kansas, so debts, lawsuits and courts reach the bunker in the same way they reach any other property.

sources.t: Cuius est solum, eius est usque ad coelum et ad inferos, Wikipedia

cases.name: Ad coelum et ad inferos
cases.anchor: No single site. Marker is London, for Blackstone's statement of the rule in England in 1766.
cases.founder: Traced to the jurist Accursius in the 13th century; William Blackstone, 1766
cases.story: The Latin phrase cuius est solum, eius est usque ad coelum et ad inferos means "whoever owns the soil, it is theirs all the way to the sky and to the depths". The maxim has been traced to the 13th-century Italian jurist Accursius, and is said to date in English common law to the time of Edward I. William Blackstone gave it its broad form in his Commentaries on the Laws of England in 1766. Modern law keeps only a limited version. Above the ground, you control the space close to your land and cannot stop flights far overhead. Below the ground, you hold subsurface rights, but in some places mineral rights beyond a set depth are separate from the land title, and the state often owns them permanently and leases them out. This is the property-law side of the question. It settles who owns a chamber or mine shaft under a plot of land, and that owner still holds it under the law of the country it lies in.
cases.mechanism: Ownership of land reaches downward as far as law allows, so anything dug below it sits inside the same property and the same country.

sources.t: Cuius est solum, eius est usque ad coelum et ad inferos, Wikipedia

cases.name: UNCLOS rules on the shelf subsoil and tunnelling
cases.anchor: No single site. Marker is UN headquarters, New York, whose law-of-the-sea office publishes the text. The rule applies on every continental shelf.
cases.founder: States party to the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea
cases.story: The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea has a section on the continental shelf, Part VI. Article 76 defines the shelf as the seabed and subsoil beyond a country's territorial sea, out to the edge of the continental margin or to 200 nautical miles from the coast where the margin stops short. Article 77 gives the coastal country sovereign rights to explore the shelf and take its natural resources. These rights are exclusive: if the country leaves them unused, nobody else may do so without its express consent. The resources covered include minerals in the subsoil. Article 85 adds that nothing in this part limits a coastal country's right to exploit the subsoil by tunnelling, however deep the water above. Deep ocean floor and its subsoil are left out of the margin. Taken together, these articles mean the coastal country's rights in the shelf subsoil hold even where the water above is open to everyone, and a private mining shaft there would need its consent.
cases.mechanism: Past the territorial sea, the subsoil of the shelf stays under the coastal state's exclusive control, including by tunnel, however free the water above it is.

sources.t: UNCLOS Part VI, Continental shelf, United Nations

cases.name: Radio Mercur
cases.anchor: Øresund, between Denmark and Sweden. A second ship later lay in the Great Belt.
cases.founder: Peer Jansen and Børge Agerskov, funded by Ib Fogh
cases.stopped_by: Danish law passed June 1962, in force 1 August 1962
cases.story: In summer 1958 Peer Jansen, a 27-year-old office trainee, and his cousin Børge Agerskov, a law student, grew tired of the conservative music on Denmark's state radio. Agerskov spotted a gap: radio in international water was regulated only by international agreements, and those had not imagined a ship broadcasting regularly from anchor. The silver trader Ib Fogh supplied money. Regular broadcasts began on 2 August 1958 from the ship Cheeta Mercur in the Øresund, carrying pop music and advertising, with programmes taped in Copenhagen and carried out by boat. A larger ship, Cheeta II, later lay in the Great Belt. It is probably the first commercial offshore radio station in the world, and it inspired Veronica, Radio Nord and others. Danish papers called it a pirate. The answer came in June 1962, when parliament banned all participation in supporting such broadcasts from 1 August, and other Nordic countries passed similar bills. The station closed officially on 31 July 1962, with a last burst in mid-August.
cases.mechanism: Denmark had no power over the ship at sea, so it made the whole supply chain on land illegal, including recording and supplying programmes.

cases.name: Radio Nord
cases.anchor: International waters of the Baltic off Stockholm; exact anchorage not given.
cases.founder: Gordon McLendon and Clint Murchison Jr., with others
cases.stopped_by: Swedish ban on selling advertising to such stations, 1962
cases.story: Radio Nord played Top 40 pop in Swedish from a ship anchored in international waters of the Baltic, with offices in central Stockholm. The Texan broadcaster Gordon McLendon and the investor Clint Murchison Jr. were among its backers. It began on 8 March 1961, six days after the Swedish Parliament passed laws letting officials seize the broadcast equipment if the ship came back to a Swedish port. The ship, first called Olga, then Bon Jour and then Magda Maria, flew the flag of Nicaragua. After Sweden pressed Nicaragua, the owners moved its registration to Panama. Sweden next banned selling advertising on the station, the part of the business that had to touch land. Radio Nord closed on 30 June 1962, a month before that law took effect. The ship sailed to Spain and was renamed Mi Amigo. In 1964 it reappeared off Essex as Radio Atlanta and then Radio Caroline South, which is already on this map.
cases.mechanism: Sweden used three levers in turn against a ship beyond its reach: a seizure power at port, pressure on the flag country, and a ban on buying its advertising.

cases.name: Radio Veronica
cases.anchor: Anchorage off Scheveningen, about a mile from the position given for Mebo II.
cases.founder: Dutch radio, TV and appliance retailers
cases.stopped_by: Dutch law in force 1 September 1974
cases.story: Dutch retailers of radios and appliances set up Radio Veronica to sell more receivers by offering an alternative to the state-licensed stations in Hilversum. Regular broadcasts began on 6 May 1960 from a former lightship, Borkum Riff, anchored off the Dutch coast. Programmes were recorded in Hilversum and taken out to it. It became the most popular station in the Netherlands. In 1964, when the Dutch government passed a law against broadcasting from REM Island, an artificial structure, it raided that island and left Veronica alone because of the station's popularity. A new ship, the trawler MV Norderney, took over that year. In May 1971 three men firebombed the rival ship Mebo II, and Veronica's directors were arrested. Parliament drew up a ban. On 2 April 1973 Norderney lost its anchor in a storm and ran aground at Scheveningen, two weeks before a planned rally, and a rival ship carried its programmes. The law passed anyway. Veronica shut at 6 pm on 31 August 1974, hours before it took effect.
cases.mechanism: The Dutch government tolerated the ship for 14 years and ended it with a law against supplying offshore stations from land.

cases.name: Radio North Sea International / Mebo II
cases.anchor: Position broadcast in the May 1971 mayday: 52°11' N, 4°16' E. The ship also lay off Clacton in 1970.
cases.founder: Edwin Bollier and Erwin Meister, Mebo Telecommunications
cases.stopped_by: Dutch Marine Offences Act, 1 September 1974
cases.story: Two Swiss engineers, Edwin Bollier and Erwin Meister, bought the 630-tonne ship Silvretta in 1969 and renamed it Mebo II. It carried a 105-kilowatt medium-wave transmitter, the strongest on any pirate ship. Regular broadcasts began on 11 February 1970. In March the ship moved to 5 miles off Clacton, in international waters. From 15 April the British government jammed it, and RNI campaigned against Labour in that June's election. It went back to the Dutch coast in July. On 29 August a tug tried to take over the ship, and the crew armed themselves with knives and petrol bombs while appealing on air. RNI closed on 24 September for 1 million guilders from Radio Veronica, then returned in January 1971. On 15 May 1971 a bomb set the ship on fire. All five people convicted got a year in prison. That attack convinced the Dutch to outlaw supplying such stations from land, effective 1 September 1974. Libya bought the ships in 1977.
cases.mechanism: States could not board a foreign-owned ship in open water, so they jammed its signal, and then cut its supply line from the shore.

cases.name: Sunk Head Fort
cases.founder: Royal Navy; abandoned 1956
cases.stopped_by: Royal Engineers demolition, 21 August 1967
cases.story: Sunk Head was one of the wartime Maunsell sea forts. It was grounded on 1 June 1942 about 18 kilometres off the Essex coast, decommissioned on 14 June 1945, and maintained until it was abandoned in 1956. Unlike some of its sister forts, it stood clearly well outside British territorial waters. That made it the same kind of site as the nearby Roughs fort, where Sealand was later declared. When the Marine, &c., Broadcasting (Offences) Act 1967 took effect in August 1967, the government wanted no broadcaster moving in. On 18 August a party from the 24th Field Squadron, Royal Engineers, under Major David Ives, boarded from the tug Collie. They weakened the structure with cutting torches and set 3,200 pounds of explosives. On 21 August the fort was blown up, and 20 feet of leg stumps remained. The demolition removed the structure before any broadcaster could occupy it.
cases.mechanism: A state that built a structure outside its waters can demolish it first, which removes the only thing a founder could have occupied there.

cases.name: SEALAB I, II and III
cases.anchor: Marker is off Bermuda, the SEALAB I site. SEALAB II lay off La Jolla, California, and SEALAB III off San Clemente Island.
cases.founder: US Navy; Captain George F. Bond
cases.stopped_by: Death of aquanaut Berry Cannon, 1969; program halted
cases.pop: 4 divers on SEALAB I; 28 on SEALAB II across teams
cases.story: The US Navy ran SEALAB to test whether people could live under pressure on the sea floor for long periods. SEALAB I went down off Bermuda on 20 July 1964 to 192 feet, with four divers planning a three-week stay, under Captain George Bond. SEALAB II followed in 1965 in the La Jolla Canyon off California. It was nearly twice the size, with hot showers and a toilet. Teams stayed 15 days, and the former astronaut Scott Carpenter stayed a record 30, with 28 divers in all. SEALAB III came four years later, 18 months late and $3 million over budget. It was lowered to 610 feet off San Clemente Island on 15 February 1969. When a seal leaked helium, divers who had been awake for twenty hours went to repair it, and Berry Cannon died on the second attempt. A Navy inquiry found his rebreather lacked the chemical that removes carbon dioxide, and a 2024 study pointed to electrocution. The program halted, and no new habitat was built.
cases.mechanism: Living on the sea floor for weeks gave the navy data on saturation diving and no legal claim to the bottom; it was a state experiment that needed a surface ship throughout.

cases.name: Conshelf / Précontinent
cases.anchor: Marker is Sha'ab Rumi off Sudan, the Conshelf Two site. Conshelf One lay off Marseille.
cases.founder: Jacques-Yves Cousteau
cases.stopped_by: Cousteau withdrew his support after Conshelf Three
cases.pop: 6 oceanauts at the main house in 1963
cases.story: Jacques Cousteau and his team set out to build an underwater village, going deeper with each project. Conshelf One, in 1962, put two divers in a small chamber 12 metres down off Marseille for two weeks. In 1963 Conshelf Two placed six oceanauts in a starfish-shaped house 10 metres down at Sha'ab Rumi in the Red Sea off Sudan, for 30 days. A hangar held a small two-man submarine, and two more men lived for a week in a "deep cabin" at 30 metres. Supplies of air, water, food and power came from the surface. Cousteau's film of it, World Without Sun, won an Academy Award. Conshelf Three followed a few years later. Cousteau then withdrew his support for this kind of use of the sea and turned to conservation. Later work showed that robots and divers sent from the surface could do the industrial jobs more efficiently, which removed the business reason for living on the bottom.
cases.mechanism: Cousteau's stations showed people could live on the shelf for a month, but they stayed tied to surface supply, and the economic case that might have paid for a permanent colony went away.

cases.name: Jules' Undersea Lodge
cases.anchor: Key Largo, Florida, at MarineLab Undersea Park.
cases.founder: Began as La Chalupa research laboratory; an exhibit there honours Ian Koblick
cases.story: This habitat began its life in the 1970s as La Chalupa, a working saturation research laboratory in Puerto Rico, used to keep scientists under pressure for long stays. It was later moved to a lagoon at Key Largo in Florida, and as Jules' Undersea Lodge it gave thousands of divers the experience of sleeping beneath the sea. Today its operator, MarineLab Undersea Park & Museum, calls it Jules' Undersea Lab. Guided dives tour it, and visitors can spend 24 hours inside on what the park calls an Aquanaut Mission. Universities and research teams can use it for diving medicine, space-analog training and marine science. The park also keeps the old MarineLab Undersea Laboratory on land as a museum piece, and an exhibit on Ian Koblick. It operates as a public attraction in a protected lagoon, with a dock, a gift shop and advance bookings, on the shore of a US state.
cases.mechanism: A habitat in a lagoon on a Florida property is simply a building under water, so state and federal law apply to it as they would on the shore.

sources.t: MarineLab Undersea Park & Museum, Home of Jules' Undersea Lab

cases.name: Aquatica
cases.anchor: No site given for Aquatica. Marker is off Key Largo, where Chamberland built an earlier two-person habitat.
cases.founder: Dennis Chamberland
cases.story: Dennis Chamberland, an aquanaut and bioengineer with thirty years at NASA, proposed a settlement on the sea floor called Aquatica. He described it as the first underwater settlement meant for permanent human colonization, and spoke of children born under water, with schools and hospitals. He had commanded seven NASA underwater missions, grown crops in controlled settings on the ocean floor, and built a two-man habitat off Key Largo that James Cameron visited. The first step, reported in February 2011, was to be a four-person underwater house called Leviathan, expected to be lowered to the seabed the following year. Its stated purpose was for residents to monitor and protect the ocean. The report gave no site, budget or legal basis, and no later report we found shows Leviathan being placed. Any seabed within reach of divers from a shore base would most likely sit on some country's continental shelf, where that country keeps its rights over the bottom.
cases.mechanism: A permanent colony on a reachable seabed would sit on a coastal state's continental shelf, which gives that state exclusive rights over the bottom and its resources, and the plan named no way around that.

sources.t: Gadling, Underwater suburbia planned in "Aquatica", 10 Feb 2011
UNCLOS Part VI, Continental shelf, United Nations

cases.name: Anton Bakov's Romanov Empire and Arca Noë
cases.anchor: No coordinates were published. Marker is off Venice, the only location stated for Arca Noë.
cases.founder: Anton Bakov
cases.stopped_by: Kiribati, the Gambia and Russia did not provide land
cases.passports: Issued online for 1,000 rubles; about 4,000 claimed by 2014
cases.story: Anton Bakov is a Russian businessman and former State Duma member who chairs the Monarchist Party. In 2011 he founded a micronation claiming to restore the Russian Empire. Under the name Imperial Throne it issued a manifesto on 31 March 2014 naming a German prince, Karl Emich of Leiningen, as Emperor Nicholas III, with Bakov as prime minister and later Archchancellor. It rebranded as the Romanov Empire in 2017. It sold passports online for 1,000 rubles, about US$31, and claimed about 4,000 by 2014. In 2013 it said it had granted citizenship to Edward Snowden. It held no land. Nicholas III asked Vladimir Putin for land in Yekaterinburg and was refused. Bakov held talks to buy territory from other states, and as of 2017 talks with Kiribati and the Gambia had failed. In 2020 he announced a successor project called Arca Noë, to be based in what he called neutral Mediterranean waters close to Venice, as part of the seasteading movement.
cases.mechanism: After several governments declined to sell or grant territory, the project moved its claim to open water, where a state's consent seemed unnecessary, and no structure has followed.

sources.t: Anton Bakov, Wikipedia (includes the Romanov Empire micronation)

cases.name: Kingdom of Romkerhall
cases.founder: Managers of the local restaurant
cases.recognition: None; a marketing title in Lower Saxony, Germany
cases.story: Romkerhall is a hotel and restaurant on the River Oker in the Harz Mountains of Germany, opposite an artificial waterfall about 64 metres high. An innkeeper named Lüer opened the first house here on 1 May 1863 on land leased from the Brunswick forestry office, and created the waterfall that same year to draw visitors. Since 1988 the managers of the restaurant have advertised the place as the "Kingdom of Romkerhall, the smallest kingdom in the world". Their reasoning rests on a real feature of German local government: the property does not belong to any municipality and sits in an unincorporated area of Goslar county in Lower Saxony. An unincorporated area of this kind has no town council of its own, yet it remains part of its county, state and Germany. The title is marketing for a hotel and waterfall.
cases.mechanism: Land outside any municipality is still inside a county and a country, so a gap in local government does not create a gap in sovereignty.

cases.name: Pangeos
cases.anchor: Marker is King Abdullah Port, Saudi Arabia, where the designers propose to build it.
cases.founder: Lazzarini, a design studio
cases.story: Pangeos is a design by the studio Lazzarini for what it calls a terayacht, shaped like a giant turtle. It would measure 550 metres long and 610 metres wide, which would make it the largest floating structure ever built, at a stated cost of $8 billion. It would hold hotels, malls, apartments, parks and ports for smaller ships and aircraft, floating on 30,000 cells, with a draft of 30 metres and solar panels on the roof. It would cruise at five knots. No yard can build it now. Around one square kilometre of sea would need to be dredged and a circular dam built, and the designers have named King Abdullah Port in Saudi Arabia as the site. They hoped to start in 2033, with a build of eight years. A crowdfunding scheme sells virtual tickets and apartments, from $16 to $169, as NFTs. A vessel of this kind would still need a flag, and nothing we read names one.
cases.mechanism: However large, a vessel at sea answers to the country whose flag it flies, so Pangeos would be a very big ship under some state's law rather than a new territory.

sources.t: CNN, Could Pangeos become the world's largest yacht?

cases.name: Maldives Floating City
cases.anchor: A Malé atoll lagoon, about 10 minutes by boat from the capital.
cases.founder: Dutch Docklands with the Government of Maldives
cases.story: Maldives Floating City is a housing project on a 200-hectare lagoon in Malé atoll, about 10 minutes by boat from the capital, promoted as an answer to rising seas. The Maldives government signed it with the Dutch developer Dutch Docklands in 2010. It stalled after a change of government in February 2012, and was signed again on 8 May 2019, when five lagoons were allotted to the company. The agreement was revised on 23 June 2022. A ministry reply reported by Atoll Times said no work had begun on the lagoons, none had been reclaimed and two had been sold, and Economy Minister Fayyaz Ismail called the project a scam. In June 2023 the company said the masterplan had changed at government request, with first prices lowered to about US$100,000, work starting that August and completion in early 2028. About 5,000 units had been planned. No mockup had been shown despite three announced dates. Other accounts give a 2027 opening for 20,000 residents. We found no report confirming finished homes.
cases.mechanism: The project rests on lagoon leases from the Maldives government, so it would stay wholly Maldivian, and floating gives it no separate legal standing.

sources.t: Atoll Times, Floating city project fails to materialise; 2 lagoons sold
Adhadhu, Floating city delayed over changes to masterplan, new completion date in 2028, 21 Jun 2023

cases.name: Kiribati's land purchase in Fiji
cases.anchor: Vanua Levu, Fiji. The estate's exact position was not given.
cases.founder: President Anote Tong, Government of Kiribati
cases.recognition: Private title in Fiji; Fiji remains sovereign
cases.story: Kiribati is a Pacific nation of low atolls. In May 2014 President Anote Tong said the government had made the final payment of US$8.6 million for the Natoavatu Estate on Vanua Levu, an island of Fiji. The 2,210-hectare property, about 22 square kilometres, had belonged to the Anglican church. Tong described it as helping with economic and food security under climate change. His environment minister said at the time they were looking for a place that could hold 60,000 or 70,000 people. Scientists rejected the reasoning, saying sand atolls can rise with the sea. Tong's successor, Taneti Maamau, later announced it would go back to being a commercial farm with technical help from China, which set off rumours it would pass to China. His office called those a fabrication, and he ruled out any military use. A country can buy land abroad this way, and what it gets is title, like any landowner, while the land stays in Fiji under Fijian law.
cases.mechanism: A state buying land in another state gets ownership and no sovereignty, so a sinking nation would still need the host's agreement to move there as a nation.

sources.t: RNZ, Kiribati completes Fiji land purchase, 28 May 2014
Kiribati and China to develop former climate-refuge land in Fiji, Yahoo News UK

cases.name: Kiribati floating-island proposal
cases.anchor: Marker is Tarawa, Kiribati. No site was named.
cases.founder: President Anote Tong
cases.recognition: Proposal by a sitting head of state
cases.story: In September 2011, at the Pacific Islands Forum meeting in New Zealand, Kiribati President Anote Tong told the Australian Broadcasting Corporation that his government was considering floating islands as an answer to rising seas. "We're considering everything including floating islands, including everything, because we are running out of options," he said. He compared the idea to oil drilling rigs and asked what any person would do if the choice was to be submerged with their family or to climb onto a rig. He put the cost at about $2 billion, money that would have to come from the international community. Three years later his government paid for land in Fiji, which is also on this map. No platform followed. The proposal came from a sitting head of state, with no site or structure attached. Under UNCLOS Article 60(8), such a platform would generate no territorial sea of its own.
cases.mechanism: A recognised state can propose moving its people to platforms, yet under UNCLOS artificial islands are not islands, so a platform would not by itself carry a state's sea zones.

sources.t: UPI via Terra Daily, Floating islands mulled as sea levels rise, 7 Sep 2011
Kiribati and China to develop former climate-refuge land in Fiji, Yahoo News UK
